title: Protocol for electron microscopy of Drosophila photoreceptor cells
protocol: Prepare the fixation buffer and keep it on ice.
Take required strains of flies and anesthetize them with carbon dioxide.
Quickly cut off the heads of the flies with a blade on a slide.
Use tweezers to expose the mouthparts of the heads.
Remove the mouthparts from the heads.
Cut the heads into two halves from the middle.
Place the tube diagonally on ice to ensure the eyes are fully immersed in fixation buffer.
Remove mouthparts quickly.
Cut heads into two halves from the middle.
Place samples gently in an Eppendorf tube using tweezers.
Add 1 mL of fixation buffer to the Eppendorf tube.
Place the Eppendorf tube on ice, keeping the eyes immersed in the buffer.
Fix samples for 20 min on ice.
Change the buffer to 1 mL of fresh fixation buffer.
Maintain all the eyes’ immersion in the new buffer.
Fix samples for 2 h on ice or 12 h at 4°C depending on eye color.
Pay attention to the appearance of bubbles during the fixation process and ensure all samples are immersed in the fixation buffer.
Wash samples by changing them into fresh 0.1 M sodium cacodylate on ice, repeating this five times for 15 minutes each time.
Ensure that all samples remain fully immersed in the 0.1 M sodium cacodylate during washing steps.
Store samples in 1 ml of fresh 0.1 M sodium cacodylate at 4°C for 12 hours after washing.
Post-fix tissues with osmium tetroxide and uranyl acetate to ensure proper fixation and good contrast under transmission electron microscope.
Wash samples in 1 mL of fresh 0.1 M sodium cacodylate in the Eppendorf tube on ice for 3 times, each for 15 min.
Fix samples with 1% osmium tetroxide solution for 1 h at 25°C in a fume hood.
Wash samples in 1 mL of fresh distilled water in the Eppendorf tube at 25°C for 5 times, each for 15 min.
Suck out the osmium tetroxide quickly after fixation is complete.
Add 1 mL of fresh distilled water and suck it out before washing.
Prepare 1 mL of 1% uranyl acetate in a fume hood carefully.
Change the samples to 1 mL of 1% uranyl acetate for 12 hours at 25°C, protected from light in a fume hood.
Wash samples in fresh distilled water in an Eppendorf tube at 25°C for 5 cycles, each lasting 15 minutes.
Suck out uranyl acetate quickly after fixation and rinse with 1 ml of fresh distilled water before washing.
Add 1 ml of 10% ethanol on ice to samples for 15 min.
Change the samples to 1 ml of 30% ethanol on ice for 15 min.
Change the samples to 1 ml of 50% ethanol on ice for 15 min.
Change the samples to 1 ml of 70% ethanol on ice for 15 min.
Change the samples to 1 ml of 85% ethanol on ice for 15 min.
Change the samples to 1 ml of 95% ethanol on ice for two cycles, each lasting 30 minutes.
Change the samples to 1 ml of absolute ethanol on ice for three cycles, each lasting 30 minutes.
Mix Spurr’s resin thoroughly in a disposable measuring beaker when dehydrating with absolute ethanol the second time.
Replace dehydrating regents in tissue with embedding regents gradually.
Change the samples to 500–800 μL of 100% propylene oxide for twice, 5 min/time.
Prepare 100% propylene oxide/Spurr’s resin mixture in an Eppendorf tube and invert the tube till they mix well.
Change the samples to 1 mL of propylene oxide/Spurr’s resin mixture and leave them cupped at 25°C in a fume hood for 12 h.
Take out the embedding mold containing the tip from the vacuum drying oven.
Prepare Spurr’s resin mixture.
Mix the Spurr’s resin in the disposable measuring beaker thoroughly for 1 h.
Change the samples to 1 mL of Spurr’s resin mixture three times, 1 hour per change, at 25°C, in a fume hood.
Cut off the pipette tip at an appropriate position with scissors.
Use the remaining pipette tip to absorb the Spurr’s resin and gently blow the samples so that they are suspended in the Spurr’s resin.
Cut off the pipette tip at the position indicated by the blue dotted line using scissors.
Use the remaining pipette tip in the square to absorb the Spurr’s resin and gently blow the eyes.
Prepare the vacuum drying oven by heating it to 65°C.
Fill with Spurr’s resin and place a compound eye in each hole of the embedding mold containing the tip.
Move the compound eye with tweezers to adjust its direction so that the most prominent part of the compound eye is as far down as possible under a stereoscopic microscope.
Place the sample in each groove of the embedding mold.
Slowly place the embedding mold into the oven at 65°C for 1 h.
Take out the embedding mold.
Fine-tune the compound eye’s direction with tweezers under a stereoscopic microscope.
Return the embedding mold to the vacuum drying oven at 65°C for 48 hours.
Trim away excess resin from the block underneath the embedded compound eye using a fresh blade under the stereomicroscope.
Shape the upper part, which contains the eye, into an equilateral trapezoid.
Glue the bottom surface of the shaped block to the cylindrical plastic base.
Adjust the initial section angle of the top surface according to the direction of the compound eye after embedding.
Rough trim the sample to reduce time spent on achieving the trapezoid face shape during sectioning.
Check the distance between the sample and the top surface to avoid cutting too close to the compound eye.
Ensure the top surface is smooth to prevent diamond sectioning knife marks.
Verify that the embedded sample is free of imperfections or debris after reaching the area of interest.
Roughen the bottom surface of the shaped block with sandpaper until it is flat.
Apply a small drop of super glue on a cylindrical plastic base.
Place the shaped resin-encased compound eye onto the base.
Glue the bottom surface of the shaped block to the cylindrical plastic base.
Allow the glue to dry before sectioning.
Place the cylindrical plastic base glued with the shaped block into the chuck on the ultramicrotome and tighten it firmly.

Set parameters on the touchscreen control panel after adjusting the direction of the block and the angle of the diamond sectioning knife, start the automated movement of the ultramicrotome specimen arm.
Place the diamond sectioning knife on the sectioning knife holder stage on the ultramicrotome.
Add a little excess water to the groove of the diamond sectioning knife to make it convex and ensure that the blade is soaked.
Allow the diamond sectioning knife to soak up distilled water for about 15 min.
A portion of the water is then slowly drawn under the microscope with a syringe or Pasteur pipette.
Adjust the lighting system so that when the liquid surface becomes concave, a curved surface reflecting light can be seen, which is the correct liquid surface and appears white under the microscope.
As the liquid evaporates during sectioning, distilled water should be added to ensure the correct liquid level.
Adjust the sample under the microscope such that the short side of the trapezoid is facing down, so that sectioning from the short edge will cause less damage to the diamond knife blade.
Adjust the knife angle so that the two parallel sides of the trapezoid are parallel to the blade.
Move the knife to align the available part with the block surface.
Raise the block until it stops slightly above the knife blade.
Set parameters in the control panel: feed of 400 nm, and a rate of 2 mm/s.
Start the automated movement of the ultramicrotome specimen arm.
Pause sectioning when a large circle (compound eye) appears in the slice.
Place the sections on the slide.
Stain the sections with 0.1% toluidine blue.
Check if the ommatidia (small circles) have been sliced using a light microscope.
Continue cutting 200 sections using a thickness parameter of 200 nm.
Clean the groove of the diamond sectioning knife and replace it with fresh distilled water.
Adjust the liquid level and sectioning parameters.
Cut sections at a speed of 1 mm/s with a thickness of 90-100 nm.
Determine section thickness according to interference color, ensuring golden sections for optimal resolution and contrast.
Stop automated movement after cutting 40 sections.
Gently move ribbon sections away from the blade using an eyelash brush.
Collect 5-6 sections on one grid carefully.
Place grids with sections into a transmission electron microscope sample box.
Stain samples with lead citrate to enhance cell membrane system and lipid contrast.
Combine uranyl acetate with most components to improve staining of nucleic acid, nuclear protein, connective tissue fiber, glycogen, secreted particles, and lysosome.
Avoid prolonged exposure to CO2 for lead citrate to prevent formation of lead carbonate precipitate.
Limit the duration of uranyl acetate staining to avoid extraction of glycogen and tissue deformation.
Prepare a parafilm of about 5 cm in width.
Place lamellar NaOH solids in rows on both sides of the parafilm.
Add a drop of 1% lead citrate between two rows of NaOH for each sample.
Insert the grid face up into the droplet containing lead citrate.
Let the grid stand for 6–8 min to allow staining.
Rinse the stained grids in Dish 1 with distilled water for 10 s.
Wash the grids in Dish 2 with distilled water for 10 s.
Wash the grids in Dish 3 with distilled water for 10 s.
Place the washed grids on filter paper to dry.
Prepare a fresh parafilm of about 5 cm in width.
Place lamellar NaOH solids in rows on both sides of the parafilm.
Add a drop of 2% uranyl acetate between two rows of NaOH for each sample.
Invert grids onto the surface of the uranyl acetate droplet using surface tension.
Leave grids on the droplet for 7–8 minutes.
Replace three dishes with fresh distilled water and wash grids for three times, each for 10 seconds.
Dry the grids on filter paper.
Place dried grids in a transmission electron microscope sample box.
Acquire images of photoreceptor cells from compound eyes using a Hitachi 7650 operated at 80 kV.
